title: Data, Charts & Averages
description: Collecting, displaying and interpreting data using bar charts, pictograms and pie charts; finding the mean, median, mode and range.

notes.heading: Collecting and Organising Data
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Data is information that has been collected, counted, or measured. In mathematics we often collect data to answer a question, compare groups, or spot patterns.

🔑 How it works
First, decide what you want to find out and write a clear question. Then collect replies using a survey, measurement, or experiment. Record the results in a frequency table: a table that lists each value or category next to how many times it occurs. Tally marks make counting easier — every fifth mark crosses the previous four like a gate: $||||$ .

When data has many different values, group it into class intervals such as $0-9$, $10-19$, $20-29$. Each interval must be the same width and must not overlap. Always include a title and clear column headings.

💡 Worked Example
Thirty students were asked how many books they read last month. The raw results were: $3, 5, 2, 5, 7, 4, 3, 6, 5, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 2, 4, 5, 7, 3, 4, 6, 5, 4, 3, 5$.

Step 1: Count each value with tally marks.
Step 2: Write the frequency table.

| Books ($x$) | Tally | Frequency ($f$) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $|||$ | 3 |
| 3 | $||||$ | 5 |
| 4 | $|||| \, |$ | 6 |
| 5 | $|||| \, ||||$ | 9 |
| 6 | $||||$ | 4 |
| 7 | $|||$ | 3 |

Total frequency $= 3 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 30$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A frequency table turns raw data into a clear summary.
• Class intervals must have equal width and no gaps.
• Always check that the total frequency matches the number of values you started with.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to make class intervals the same width. Intervals like $0-10$, $10-20$, $20-30$ are fine, but $0-10$, $11-15$, $16-30$ are not because the widths are different and comparisons become misleading.

notes.heading: Bar Charts
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A bar chart displays categorical or discrete numerical data using rectangular bars. The height of each bar shows the frequency, and the labels on the horizontal axis show the categories.

🔑 How it works
Every bar must have the same width and the same-sized gap between bars. The vertical axis must start at zero; otherwise the differences between bars look bigger or smaller than they really are. Bars can be drawn horizontally or vertically.

💡 Worked Example
A class recorded favourite fruits:

| Fruit | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Apple | 8 |
| Banana | 12 |
| Grapes | 5 |
| Orange | 7 |

Step 1: Draw the axes and label them: horizontal axis = Fruit, vertical axis = Frequency.
Step 2: Choose a sensible scale. Here the highest frequency is 12, so count up to 14 in steps of 2.
Step 3: Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps. Apple rises to 8, Banana to 12, Grapes to 5, Orange to 7.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bar height = frequency.
• Equal widths and equal gaps keep the chart fair.
• The vertical axis should usually start at 0.
• Always give the chart a title and label both axes.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Students sometimes read the top of a bar correctly but forget to check the scale. If one small square represents 2 people, a bar reaching three small squares above 10 actually represents 16 people, not 13.

notes.heading: Pictograms and Pie Charts
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A pictogram uses pictures or symbols to represent data. A pie chart uses sectors of a circle to show how a whole amount is divided into parts.

🔑 How it works — Pictograms
Each symbol stands for a fixed number of items, shown in the key. Always check the key before counting. If ★ = 4 books, then ★★★½ represents $3.5 \times 4 = 14$ books.

🔑 How it works — Pie Charts
A full turn is 360°. The angle for each sector is found by:
$$\text{sector angle} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total frequency}} \times 360^\circ$$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Pictogram
A key says 🚲 = 10 students. If the row for 'walk' shows 🚲🚲🚲½, the number of students who walk is $3.5 \times 10 = 35$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Pie Chart
In a survey of 40 students, 10 chose tennis. The tennis sector angle is:
$$\frac{10}{40} \times 360^\circ = 90^\circ$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Pictograms: read the key first; half or quarter symbols are common.
• Pie charts: each sector angle is proportional to the frequency.
• Pie charts are best for showing proportions, not exact amounts.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing a pie chart without checking that all the sector angles add up to 360°. If they do not, a calculation error has been made.

notes.heading: The Mean
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The mean is the average found by sharing the total equally among all the values. It uses every value in the data set.

🔑 How it works
Add all the values together, then divide by how many values there are:
$$\text{mean} = \frac{\text{sum of values}}{\text{number of values}}$$

💡 Worked Example 1
Find the mean of $4, 7, 9, 12, 13$.

Step 1: Add the values.
$4 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 13 = 45$

Step 2: Count the values.
There are 5 values.

Step 3: Divide.
$\text{mean} = 45 \div 5 = 9$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Mean from a frequency table
| Value ($x$) | Frequency ($f$) | $x \times f$ |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 3 | 6 |
| 3 | 5 | 15 |
| 4 | 2 | 8 |

Total frequency $= 3 + 5 + 2 = 10$
Total of $x \times f = 6 + 15 + 8 = 29$
$\text{mean} = 29 \div 10 = 2.9$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The mean is sometimes just called the average.
• It is affected by every value, including very large or very small ones.
• When using a frequency table, multiply each value by its frequency before adding.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing by the number of different values instead of the total frequency. In Worked Example 2 there are three different values but ten values altogether, so we divide by 10.

notes.heading: The Median and the Mode
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order. The mode is the value that appears most often.

🔑 How it works — Median
1. Arrange the values in order from smallest to largest.
2. If there is an odd number of values, the median is the middle one.
3. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.

🔑 How it works — Mode
Count how many times each value appears. The value with the highest frequency is the mode. A data set can have more than one mode or no mode at all.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Median with odd count
Data: $8, 3, 7, 5, 9$
In order: $3, 5, 7, 8, 9$
The middle value is 7, so median $= 7$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Median with even count
Data: $6, 2, 9, 5$
In order: $2, 5, 6, 9$
Two middle values are 5 and 6.
$\text{median} = \frac{5 + 6}{2} = 5.5$

💡 Worked Example 3 — Mode
Data: $4, 7, 4, 9, 7, 4, 2$
4 appears three times, 7 appears twice, 9 and 2 appear once.
Mode $= 4$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The median is not affected much by extreme values.
• The mode is the only average that can be used with non-numerical data.
• If two values tie for highest frequency, the data is bimodal.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Picking the median from the original unordered list. You must arrange the values in order first.

notes.heading: The Range and Outliers
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The range measures how spread out the data is. It is the largest value minus the smallest value:
$$\text{range} = \text{maximum} - \text{minimum}$$

🔑 Key Concept
A large range tells us the values are spread out. A small range tells us the values are close together. An outlier is a value that is very different from the rest of the data. Outliers can pull the mean up or down, but they usually have little effect on the median or mode.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Range
Data: $12, 8, 15, 3, 10$
Maximum $= 15$, minimum $= 3$
$\text{range} = 15 - 3 = 12$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Effect of an outlier
Data without outlier: $5, 6, 6, 7, 8$
Mean $= 32 \div 5 = 6.4$, median $= 6$, mode $= 6$.

Add an outlier of 50: $5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 50$
Mean $= 82 \div 6 \approx 13.7$ (much higher)
Median $= (6 + 7) \div 2 = 6.5$ (hardly changed)
Mode $= 6$ (unchanged)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Range only uses two values, so one outlier can make the range misleadingly large.
• When data has outliers, the median often gives a better typical value than the mean.
• Always report an average together with a measure of spread such as the range.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Thinking the range is a type of average. It is not; it describes spread, not a typical value.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Average and Reading Charts
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An average is a single value that represents a typical value in a data set. The best average depends on the data and the question you are trying to answer.

🔑 How it works
Use the mean when the data is fairly symmetrical and has no extreme values. Use the median when there are outliers or when the data is skewed. Use the mode for categorical data or when you want the most common answer. Always pair an average with the range or another measure of spread.

💡 Worked Example — Choosing an average
A small shop records daily takings for a week: £120, £135, £128, £140, £132, £125, £800.

Mean = £1580 ÷ 7 ≈ £225.71
Median = £132 (middle value of ordered list)
Mode: no value repeats.

The £800 day is an outlier. The mean makes the shop look much busier than usual, so the median (£132) is a fairer typical daily taking.

✅ Check — Reading charts
Before answering any chart question:
1. Read the title.
2. Check the labels on both axes.
3. Look at the scale and what each unit represents.
4. Read the key if it is a pictogram or pie chart.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Mean: uses every value; affected by outliers.
• Median: middle value; robust against outliers.
• Mode: most common; useful for categories.
• Range: shows spread; use alongside an average.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'the chart shows...' without quoting numbers. In mathematics you must back up statements with values from the data or chart.

questions.explanation: The sum is $6 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 14 = 50$. There are 5 values, so the mean is $50 \div 5 = 10$.
Arrange in order: $1, 3, 5, 7, 9$. The middle value is 5, so the median is 5.
The value 7 appears three times, which is more often than any other value, so the mode is 7.
Range = maximum − minimum. The maximum is 19 and the minimum is 3, so $19 - 3 = 16$.
Arrange in order: $18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 30$. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: $(22 + 24) \div 2 = 23$.

questions.stem: The heights of four students are $120\text{ cm}, 115\text{ cm}, 130\text{ cm}, 127\text{ cm}$. What is the mean height?
A survey of 30 students found 15 prefer blue, 9 prefer red, and 6 prefer green. What is the pie chart angle for blue?
A pictogram uses ★ = 4 books. How many books are represented by ★★★½?
questions.explanation: Three full stars represent $3 \times 4 = 12$ books. Half a star represents $4 \div 2 = 2$ books. Total $= 12 + 2 = 14$ books.

questions.stem: Scores: $8, 7, 9, 6, 10$. A new score of 2 is added. Which average is most affected?
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so adding the outlier 2 pulls the mean down significantly. The median changes only slightly and there is still no mode.

questions.stem: Which type of chart is best for showing the proportions of a whole?
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows how a total is divided into parts, making proportions easy to compare at a glance.

questions.stem: The mean of four test scores is 72. After a fifth test, the mean rises to 76. What was the fifth test score?
questions.explanation: Total of first four scores $= 4 \times 72 = 288$. Total of five scores $= 5 \times 76 = 380$. Fifth score $= 380 - 288 = 92$.

questions.stem: For the data set $2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 8, 14$, which statement is true?
choices: The mean is 6, the median is 5, and the mode is 3.
The mean is 5, the median is 3, and the mode is 7.
The mean is 6, the median is 3, and the mode is 5.
The mean is 5, the median is 5, and the mode is 3.
questions.explanation: Mean $= (2 + 3 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 8 + 14) \div 7 = 42 \div 7 = 6$. Median $= 5$ (the middle value when ordered). Mode $= 3$ (appears twice).

questions.stem: A bar chart shows the number of pets owned by students. The scale goes up in steps of 5, and the bar for 'dog' reaches halfway between 15 and 20. How many dogs are there?
questions.explanation: Halfway between 15 and 20 on a scale going up in fives represents $17.5$. Since the scale step is 5, the half-way mark is $15 + 2.5 = 17.5$.

questions.stem: Five students' quiz scores are $7, 9, 6, 8, 10$. What is their mean score?
questions.explanation: Sum $= 7 + 9 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 40$. There are 5 scores, so mean $= 40 \div 5 = 8$.

questions.stem: A small café records daily customers for a week: $45, 48, 50, 47, 49, 46, 120$. Which average best represents a typical day?
choices: Mean, because it uses every value
Median, because the 120 is an outlier
Range, because it shows the spread
questions.explanation: The value 120 is much higher than the others, so it pulls the mean up. The median gives a fairer typical value because it is not strongly affected by the outlier. Range is a measure of spread, not an average.
